title: The Speak & Spell
hook: A 1978 spelling toy was the first to fit a whole speech synthesizer on one chip.
peek: Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell read words aloud and asked children to spell them. Its talking voice came from a single chip that rebuilt speech from compact codes, and the toy later turned up in E.T. and in electronic music.
lede: In 1978 Texas Instruments released the Speak & Spell, a bright orange toy that said a word aloud and asked a child to type its spelling. Talking machines then usually needed racks of equipment. TI's engineers squeezed the job onto a single chip, the TMS5100, making it the first single-chip speech synthesizer. It went into a toy sold in shops.

bullets.text: Instead of storing recordings, the chip used linear predictive coding. It modelled the human vocal tract as a changing filter and stored just a few numbers per moment of speech, so whole words fit in a tiny memory.
The project was led by a small team of TI engineers: Paul Breedlove, Richard Wiggins, Larry Brantingham and Gene Frantz. Wiggins worked on the speech maths, while Brantingham designed the chip.
In the 1982 film E.T., the alien builds a communicator to call home, and a Speak & Spell is part of it. The scene made the toy famous with a new generation.
Musicians love its odd, robotic voice. Kraftwerk used one, and the inventor of circuit bending, Reed Ghazala, rewired Speak & Spells to make strange new sounds.
